motion: women will be worse off after the Arab revolutions

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: If women can organize, speak publicly, and challenge new leaders, why should that greater power count as a worsening of their position rather than a route to lasting improvement?

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: I grant that public voice can help some women. But voice without safety, income, or enforceable rights is not power; it is exposure. When protection collapses first, women can be worse off after revolutions.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to this debate on whether women will be worse off after the Arab revolutions. Andreas takes the motion, and Gareth opposes it. Each debater has thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. I will give a ten-second cue, then each has thirty seconds to close.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Women may gain a vote, yet lose safety, work, and influence when old controls collapse. Revolutions often remove weak protections before building stronger ones. The question is not whether change sounds hopeful, but whether women actually hold more power afterward. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: All right, let's give Gareth a chance to reply.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I reject that forecast because revolutions can break the bargains that kept women excluded. New public debate gives women room to organize, demand rights, and challenge officials. Some protections may weaken briefly, but that does not mean women will be worse off overall.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Greater voice and public pressure can produce stronger rights, not lasting loss. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Now we go on to round two. And round two is where the debaters address one another directly. This round runs two and a half minutes from the moment I finish. I will call ten seconds before the end.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I accept that some old restrictions may survive. But if revolutions open political space, why assume women gain protection rather than lose the fragile safeguards they had? The upheaval itself can make women worse off.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I do not assume women gain automatically; I reject the idea that upheaval proves loss. When women organize openly, they can press for rights that old systems never allowed, so the likely direction is improvement.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That raises a neighbouring policy question: should new governments rebuild services before expanding political competition? If they chase constitutional change while leaving schools, courts, and workplaces weak, public promises become slogans, and citizens lose trust in reform.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, again, it's not on our topic about women will be worse off after the Arab revolutions.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The motion asks whether women become worse off after these revolutions, and weak courts and services make that outcome more likely. Political openings do not protect women when institutions cannot enforce their rights.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A related issue is whether new leaders can govern at all while institutions are being rebuilt. That uncertainty matters, but it does not settle our question. Women are not worse off when new participation lets them demand enforcement.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I believe no revolution should ever leave women worse off. Yet revolutions can remove limits on abuse before replacing them, so women may face greater danger and less security after the old order falls.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I accept that danger can rise during disorder. But your main claim treats the first shock as the final result; when women gain a public voice, they can push institutions toward protection, so women are not worse off.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This revolution should leave women worse off. Its leaders can promise equality while shifting burdens onto women, weakening household security, and leaving formal rights without practical protection.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You said no revolution should ever leave women worse off, but you see it as this revolution should leave women worse off.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The two statements fit as a moral rule and a warning about reality: revolutions should protect women, yet this revolution can still fail them. That failure is precisely why the aftermath may make women worse off.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your weakest point is calling a warning a forecast. You offer no reason this revolution must fail, and you ignore women using new public space to resist that failure and improve their position.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, and then closing statements.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine a woman whose local protection disappears, whose work becomes unsafe, and whose complaint reaches no functioning court. A promised right cannot help her then; that concrete loss shows-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time's up. First, onto round three, closing statements from each debater in turn. First, to summarize his position in favor of the motion, Andreas.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This motion turns on lived power, not hopeful promises. If women lose safety and enforceable rights while institutions are rebuilt, a new voice cannot offset that harm. Revolutions may open doors, but women are worse off when those doors lead to insecurity. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Gareth, the floor is yours.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The motion asks us to predict the whole aftermath, not freeze women at the first moment of disorder. Revolutions can weaken old barriers and create public space for women to organize. That power can demand better laws and stronger institutions. We should judge the direction of change, not only its early risks.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Women are not doomed to lose when political space expands. They can turn new visibility into pressure, rights, and protection. The evidence offered here shows danger, not a lasting verdict-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Gareth. Your time is up.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for taking part. This debate is now closed without declaring a winner.
